speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This approach has served us well, as Singapore's banking system has remained resilient in the face of the Global Financial Crisis of 2008.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Following the crisis, MAS has been actively involved in coordinated efforts among international regulators to strengthen capital and liquidity standards for banks, and to create a more robust international banking system.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Likewise within Singapore, MAS has been refining the regulatory and supervisory framework to strengthen the resilience of our financial institutions and to enhance the stability of the financial system as a whole.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this Banking (Amendment) Bill forms part of the overall effort.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MAS has consulted extensively with the industry and the public on the policy changes and the draft Bill.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It has studied the feedback received and incorporated it into the Bill where appropriate.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, to strengthen prudential safeguards and enhance depositor protection.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, a foreign bank can choose to operate in Singapore as a branch or a locally incorporated subsidiary.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A bank branch will rely on support from its head office, which is subject to capital and other requirements imposed by its home regulator on a group basis.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In contrast, a locally incorporated subsidiary will have its own capital and be subject to MAS' capital and other regulatory requirements.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This new regulatory power forms part of the suite of policy measures for domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs).

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This was announced by MAS in April last year.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The subsidiary will then be subject to MAS' own regulatory requirements, based on its risk profile.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill will also empower MAS to impose prudential requirements that cap banks' leverage and ensure that they maintain sufficient liquidity.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As I mentioned earlier, MAS has always maintained high standards of prudential regulation and supervision for our banks; in fact, somewhat higher than in most other jurisdictions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Over the years, we have developed a system of regulation that allows well-managed risk-taking and innovation, ensuring the stable and sustainable development of the financial services sector.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This Bill will update our rules to reflect new international standards, which MAS has been involved in shaping through its participation in various international financial forums.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The second purpose of the Bill is to strengthen the corporate governance of banks.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Effective corporate governance plays a critical role in ensuring robust risk management, decision-making Page: 100 and accountability within banks.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The grounds of removal will be aligned with the criteria for approving their appointments.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To enhance MAS' oversight of these appointments, the Bill will require banks to notify MAS as soon as they become aware of any material information which may negatively affect the fitness or propriety of any director or executive officer whose appointment was approved by MAS.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill will also repeal the provision that makes bank directors jointly and severally liable for any bank losses arising from credit facilities or exposures to the directors and their related parties.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This provision was intended to emphasise the fiduciary duty that bank directors owed to their bank.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: However, based on feedback provided by the banks, this provision discourages candidates from taking up bank directorships and more importantly, MAS has also assessed that it does not provide effective oversight over banks' related party transactions (RPTs).

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Instead, to address the potential conflicts of interest arising from RPTs, MAS will require a bank to conduct all such transactions on an arm's length basis and to obtain board approval before entering into such transactions that pose material risks to the bank.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill will also enhance MAS' powers to direct a bank to terminate, prohibit and restrict transactions that the bank enters into with its related parties, if these are deemed detrimental to depositors' interests.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill will also enhance corporate governance of banks by reinforcing the complementary role of external auditors in assessing a bank's risks and internal controls.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will be done through a few key measures, such as the introduction of a safe harbour provision to protect banks' external auditors from liability where they disclose confidential information to MAS as part of their reporting obligations under the Banking Act.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Furthermore, MAS will be empowered to direct a bank to remove its external auditors if they have not discharged their statutory duties satisfactorily.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is the third broad area of amendments.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These amendments will formalise MAS' expectation that banks establish risk management systems and controls that are commensurate with their business profiles and operations.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MAS will be able to impose penalties on banks that fail to do so.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will allow MAS to exercise better oversight of banks' activities at such locations.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, MAS will be able to require a bank to institute adequate safeguards against money laundering and terrorism financing, before it can commence money-changing and remittance businesses at new locations.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Besides these three broad areas which I have just outlined, there are also several significant amendments to update the banking regulatory framework.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the case of a bank incorporated in Singapore, this extends to any adverse developments that may materially affect related entities of the bank.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will allow MAS to take the necessary supervisory action in a timely manner.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It will also allow the parent supervisory authority of a foreign bank or merchant bank to inspect all financial activities of the bank or merchant bank in Singapore, upon Page: 101 MAS' approval.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the parent based overseas can inspect the financial activities of the bank or merchant bank in Singapore, subject to MAS' approval.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These changes will facilitate the consolidated supervision of internationally active banks and merchant banks.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These amendments to the Banking Act will help strengthen the banking industry and align our regulatory regime with international best practices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Global Financial Crisis showed the world how high the stakes are in getting our banking regulatory frameworks right.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having said this, we must ensure the continued competitiveness of our banking sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore's financial services sector makes a very significant contribution to jobs and the gross domestic product (GDP) in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Regulations should be framed and implemented in such a way as to minimise ambiguity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would ensure that banks do not "overegg the pudding" so as to drive up compliance costs that could end up being passed onto the end-customers of banking products, not to mention crimping the job creation engine of the sector, however slightly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this context, while supporting the Bill, I would like to pose a few clarifying questions and make some suggestions with respect to implementing specific provisions of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If MAS uses this power to direct a bank to terminate a transaction with its related party, for example, that act could conceivably result in a financial loss much bigger than the $250,000 fine that is associated with this provision.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a decision could also inflict reputational damage on the bank.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In relation to this provision – clause 17 – there is a risk that if banks do not clearly understand the guidelines which MAS will use to exercise its power to terminate transactions or eliminate exposures, this may create a culture of excessive notification and consultation with MAS at best, or excessive risk-aversion at worst.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Page: 102 The Bill also requires banks to immediately notify MAS of any developments that would adversely and materially affect its financial soundness, reputation and ability to conduct business.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In relation to this provision – clause 34 – there is a risk that if the banks do not clearly understand what needs and what does not need to be reported to MAS, this will create a burden of excessive notification which may raise compliance costs, however slightly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And these compliance costs may end up being passed onto end-consumers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will MAS, for instance, be publishing a guidance document on how it will operationalise these powers, similar to the guidance published on anti-money laundering and terrorism finance last year and private banking controls in 2014?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moving onto the next part of my speech, there are certain provisions in the Bill which I do not oppose.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nevertheless, these provisions would give MAS additional powers over banks and in some cases, these powers may lengthen the turnaround time for decisions, limit business flexibility and, therefore, raise the cost of doing business, however slightly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, in the interest of transparency, I would like to pose some questions to better understand – and for the banking community and stakeholders to better understand – the Government's thinking in relation to these issues and to ask what facts prompted the Government to include these provisions in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This information may be relevant to other national sectors, other than just the banking sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would be helpful for the public to better understand what facts MAS is detecting about such practices by banking businesses as it may have implications for other sectors of society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For instance, is MAS detecting overly aggressive marketing practices for credit or charge cards that may be fuelling unsustainable over-spending by at-risk families?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, it would be useful to highlight this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Non-government organisations and voluntary welfare organisations working with at-risk families and at-risk individuals could help to provide feedback to MAS if they notice such unhealthy card marketing practices on the ground.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This could help MAS to decide which locations are appropriate locations to allow credit or charge card-related or marketing activities, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill also requires banks to seek MAS approval for changing locations or adding locations for non-banking activities, including money-changing and remittance services, as the Minister observed in his speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unlike wealth management products under the Financial Advisers Act with risk of capital loss, money-changing and remittance are considered non-banking activities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Once again, I would like to ask what facts or trends have prompted the Government to impose a requirement that banks seek the approval of MAS for location choice for these non-banking activities, as opposed to just notifying MAS.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To Mr Leon Perera's point on having card institutions needing to seek the approval of MAS for conduct of business in certain jurisdictions, I actually support the point because my credit card just had a charge from Azerbaijan and I have no idea how it came forth.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, I do support having MAS put in more controls on credit card companies' places of business.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These past few years have seen the rise of new financing arrangements and initiatives, providing businesses with alternatives to obtaining loans from banks or personal contacts.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The specific arrangements that I would like to focus on today are the peer-to-peer lending platforms (P2P platforms).

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Very briefly, a company that wants to take a loan approaches the platform, which then offers the opportunity to its members.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Members can choose to offer as much or as little as they are comfortable lending, within the guidelines of the platform.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The platform will then aggregate contributions from many individual lenders into one single large loan to the company.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Growth in the United Kingdom (UK) has been similarly explosive, with business P2P lending growing sevenfold from £200 million in 2013 to £1.5 billion in 2015.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: P2P lending is an example of the transformative power of the Internet – the business model simply could not work without fast and efficient communication and the ability to transact with multiple individuals.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For upcoming businesses, it opens up new channels for funding, given that banks are typically reluctant to lend to companies with a limited track record.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Harnessing the "wisdom of crowds", individual lenders offering smaller sums could be better at allocating capital towards future potential, thereby improving the odds of success for the startups and small and medium enterprises (SMEs) that we need to drive our economy forward.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For lenders, such platforms offer a rare chance for them to earn higher returns on their money, typically above 10%, albeit with higher risks.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, as with any new financial innovation, this raises concern about the appropriate extent of regulation, in order to both safeguard the financial system and protect the interests of lenders.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: MAS is currently in the process of drafting the required regulations and, hence, the platforms are effectively operating in a regulatory vacuum.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We understand, of course, that the speed of innovation can make it challenging for the regulatory authorities to keep up.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the same time, an appropriate regulatory regime is urgently needed to reduce uncertainty and maximise benefits for all parties.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What are the key elements of an appropriate regulatory framework for P2P lending?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we start from the perspective of risks, P2P lending seems unlikely to be a source of systemic threat to the overall banking system in Singapore, at least for now, given that they are still small in comparison to commercial banks.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The greatest risk, therefore, falls on the individual lenders, who risk losing all or part of their investment if the loan goes into default before the principal is repaid.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How should Page: 104 we protect such individuals without inadvertently introducing moral hazard by creating the impression that such loans are iron-clad and can never go wrong?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The key piece of regulation should focus on preventing fraud by the platform.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On the other hand, we need to ensure that the platforms have systems in place to prevent money laundering.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This suggests the need for a licensing regime to ensure that the proper processes and accountability systems are in place at the platforms.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A clear licensing regime helps reduce uncertainty and ambiguity on the part of the platforms.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, given that these companies will often be themselves startups, the requirements should not be so onerous as to stifle innovation.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Regulations should not go so far as to eliminate all risk from the transaction, as that would itself create unhealthy behaviours as people chase high interest rates while assuming they will be protected should something go wrong.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is also the need to balance access and protection.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If, as has been proposed, we restrict participation to Accredited Investors or Institutions, we would be protecting the average man in the street, but also preventing them from accessing a potentially beneficial asset class.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Here, we can take inspiration from the various consumer protection rules already in place across the financial industry, such as "cooling-off periods" where they can change their minds without penalty.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will, hopefully, reduce the risk that retail investors might invest in inappropriate products.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One key area is to ensure that the lenders are able to collectively pursue action should there be a default, just as any institutional creditor would.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Each individual share may be too small to find it worthwhile to bear the cost and effort of pursuing a claim.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Hence, collective instruments for protecting the interests of all lenders need to be put in place.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By addressing the concerns of potential lenders, this will, in turn, help convince more to participate and accelerate the growth of the industry.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Like it or not, technological innovation in the financial industry is going to grow and we should not stand in the way of initiatives that facilitate the creation of good businesses and jobs.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What is important is to make sure the public is well-informed and that the P2P lenders operate in a regulatory environment that provides clear guidelines without being overly burdensome.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I would, first, address Mr Leon Perera's point about finding the right balance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I fully agree with the Member that there is a need to find a balance between ensuring adequate prudential safeguards and ensuring the competitiveness of the financial sector in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I hope the Member agrees that we have, in fact, been doing so over the past few years, and we have managed it, I think, better than most other financial jurisdictions, if we look at it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: After the Global Financial Crisis in 2008, we saw many global financial institutions downsizing their global operations significantly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Singapore has not been spared, but I would say, if we look at the scale of the downsizing at the international level, the impact on Singapore has been relatively contained.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This shows that while we have taken a path to find a balance with adequate strong safeguards, we also ensure that our financial sector is competitive and able to retain good jobs and generate good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the other points that the Member raised, I will address them specifically.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On new requirements, the Member mentioned clauses 17 and 34 on related party transactions and the need for guidelines and the concerns over burden and compliance costs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS has been very mindful of ensuring that it does not add unnecessary compliance costs for banks and that is why I am coming up with this set of amendments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS consulted the industry extensively and, where appropriate, had, indeed, made adjustments to the requirements.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we have repealed an existing provision which we have assessed to be not so effective.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Instead, we have put in place other requirements to ensure and safeguard against related party transactions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS will, certainly, be mindful of implementing this well and providing sufficient transition time to the banks to make sure that they are able to have sufficient time to transit to meet the new requirements.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Leon Perera had suggested having prescribed or detailed guidelines.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS will consider this, but it is not always possible to prescribe each and every scenario where there are related party transactions, because there could be many circumstances under which they can happen.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, in some instances, it may be based on principles that are set out, and adequate consultation and engagement will be done with the banks to ensure that they are able to implement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is the same approach we will take with regard to the initiatives or new provisions that Mr Perera had highlighted.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: He mentioned clause 46 with regard to place of business and the concerns that this may raise the cost of doing business.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: He also asked whether there were any trends, in particular, that had sparked off such a new provision.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS is looking at how we can do it in a more comprehensive way and to, again, ensure that we maintain our high prudential standards.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Member had suggested that this can be done just through notification.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But notification alone may not be sufficient for MAS and will not give MAS the powers to act just on the basis of a notification.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are new and necessary measures that are needed to ensure that our prudential standards are maintained and held to a high standard.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I would also add that many of the new measures that are being proposed are not just being done by MAS alone, but they are also measures that are done internationally.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are not done unilaterally by us, but they are measures that have been discussed in international financial forums which MAS has been active in.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS has also played an active role in shaping these international standards, which are progressively being implemented in other jurisdictions as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon talked about a new area of risk on P2P lending.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is potentially a benefit as well as an opportunity but, as he highlighted, it is also a new area of risk.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I should, at the outset, clarify that P2P activities are not directly within the scope of the Banking Act, which focuses on the regulatory framework for banks involved in the business of taking deposits and lending funds.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, P2P lending may not be directly covered within the scope of the Banking Act.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is an area which is new, and it is a new form of financing globally.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Within Singapore it is still at a nascent stage.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But it is an area which is gaining more interest and attention, and we are certainly paying attention to it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As the Member had noted, while these platforms add to the diversity of the financial landscape, investors participating in P2P platforms should be aware of the risks, and there are considerable risks involved.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These include risks that the crowdfunding proposals may be fraudulent or that the promised returns do not materialise.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Also, it is because crowdfunding is commonly used by startup businesses to raise funds for the initial stages of a business cycle, lenders would also be exposed to the higher failure rates associated with startups.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, these are the risks involved in P2P lending.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we must strike a balance between investor protection and innovation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why with this balance in mind, MAS had put up a consultation paper that the Member had alluded to.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It was a consultation paper on securities-based crowdfunding.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I believe I have addressed their questions and I hope that Members will support the amendment Bill that is being tabled.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is the objective of the Banking Act amendments we have proposed today.
